source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension / Directorate General of Agriculture, "បច្ចេកទេសដាំដុះសណ្តែកសៀង" [Soybean cultivation techniques], official extension manual, 2018
text:
Disease section (labeled "អំពីជំងឺ និងសត្វល្អិត" — Diseases and Insects) covers three main diseases with photos and named causal organisms:

- Leaf spot (ជំងឺអុចស្លឹក), caused by Cercospora sojina: circular brown-bordered lesions on leaves that can coalesce and cause premature leaf drop and reduced yield in severe cases; control recommendations include using healthy/clean seed, crop rotation, avoiding dense planting that keeps humidity high around foliage, removing and destroying crop residue after harvest, and applying fungicides where the disease is established — the manual names Captan, Carboxin, Thiabendazole, and Thiran as older-generation options and Difenoconazole, azoxystrobin, propiconazole, and Chlorothalonil as newer systemic/broader-spectrum options.
- Powdery mildew (ជំងឺម្សៅសដែម), caused by Microsphaera diffusa: white powdery fungal growth on leaf surfaces, most damaging when infection occurs early and spreads before flowering; the same general cultural controls apply, with fungicides named including Mancozeb, Metalaxyl, Hexaconazole, and Tebuconazole for cases needing chemical control.
- Bean yellow mosaic virus (the source's own Khmer disease name was visible but not fully legible to transcribe with confidence and is omitted here per project convention): a viral mosaic disease transmitted by thrips, hopper, and aphid vectors, causing leaf yellowing/mottling, distorted growth, and reduced pod set; the manual's control advice is centered on managing the insect vectors (removing infected plants promptly, avoiding planting near existing infected legume fields, keeping fields weed-free since many weeds host both the virus and its vectors, and applying an insecticide targeted at the vector insects where vector pressure is high — Thiamethoxam, buprofezin, chlorpyrifos, and imidacloprid are named as vector-control options) since there is no direct chemical cure for the virus itself once a plant is infected.
